items.caption: This oracle-script style redraw of 東 has a tall enclosing outline with several interior openings. A database interprets early forms as a tied bag, though that proposed original sense remains disputed.
items.alt: Black oracle-script style character with a tall, rounded enclosure and several white openings.
items.selection_reason: A useful early graphic example for the proposed bag interpretation; its visible structure can be described without treating the drawn openings as proof of what the graph depicted.

items.caption: This Shang bronze-script style redraw of 東 has a rounded outer contour crossed by horizontal and vertical strokes, creating a grid-like interior. The file page associates it with the late-Shang 東父乙尊; the sack interpretation of early forms is disputed.
items.alt: Black rounded bronze-script style form with crossing interior strokes and multiple openings.
items.selection_reason: Its distinct, grid-like interior provides a useful early-form comparison alongside the oracle-style candidate. It is a modern redraw associated by its file page with a named bronze source, not an artifact photograph.

items.caption: This seal-script style redraw of 東 has a rounded central enclosure divided by horizontal and vertical strokes, with strokes extending above and below. Shuowen records an interpretation involving 日 within 木; that historical explanation does not establish the graph's earliest origin.
items.alt: Black seal-script style form with a divided rounded center and strokes extending above and below.
items.selection_reason: The form makes a useful comparison for the historically influential Shuowen explanation, while the visible shape and that account do not settle the graph’s early origin.

limitations.text: These are modern vector redraws rather than photographs of ancient inscriptions. Early forms are interpreted as a tied bag in some analyses, but this account is disputed, and the surviving evidence does not establish the depicted object's spoken name or prove the proposed sound-loan pathway to “east.”
Shuowen preserves a historical 日-within-木 interpretation; it is not confirmation that the graph originated as a sun-and-tree compound.
